It's June 2032. Andrei is looking for work in Berlin. Lena has found an advert: the BVG, Berlin's transport company, is looking for a software developer for its tram app. Ludwig is thrilled.
Andrei, listen: “The Berlin transport company is looking for a software developer, to start as soon as possible, to develop the passenger app.” That's you!
Show me. “Your profile: a completed degree in computer science, experience with mobile apps, a very good knowledge of German.” Hm. The German part worries me.
You speak German better than half of Prenzlauer Berg. And the BVG! My boy, that's my old company. I was at the BVG for forty years.
Unfortunately that doesn't help me with the CV. How do you write one in Germany? In Romania we write full sentences.
Not here. A German CV is a table. On the left the period, on the right the stage. And no full sentences, but nouns: “Studies in computer science”, not “I studied computer science”.
And the photo? In some countries it's not allowed.
In Germany it's no longer compulsory, but many people still include one. A friendly photo, not a holiday one. And not the one with flour on your face.
And what do I write in the cover letter? That I bake bread every morning at four?
Why not? It shows you're reliable and can work under pressure. Those are the two words every HR manager wants to hear.
And write why the BVG in particular. Not just because you need a job. But because…
…because I live with a man who drove trams for forty years and tells me every evening everything that's wrong with the app?
Exactly that. It's the best motivation there is.
We are looking, as soon as possible, for…

The usual order is reverse chronological (most recent at the top). Dates are written “MM/YYYY”. At the end: place, date and signature.
In a CV you don't write “Ich habe … studiert”, but “Studium der …”. German marks go from 1 (very good) to 6: a mark of “1,4” is excellent!
In CVs and official texts, verbs become nouns:
Nouns ending in -ung are always feminine: die Entwicklung, die Leitung. Infinitives used as nouns are neuter: das Programmieren.

It took Andrei a week to do his application. He wrote the CV in one evening, with Lena's help, and was amazed at how short his life looked in a table: twelve lines. Born in 2003 in Sibiu. School, school-leaving exam, bachelor's degree, Erasmus, master's. Languages: Romanian, German, English. Hobbies: reading, hiking, baking bread. “Is that me?” he asked Lena. “Twelve lines?” Lena laughed. “No. That's just what fits in a table. The rest goes in the cover letter.”

The next morning, at half past four, Andrei was in the café's bakery as he was every day, kneading dough. He was thinking about the twelve lines. Between “master's” and “languages” so much was missing: the night on the train to Sibiu, his grandfather's workshop, the fifty-second bird with the crooked eyes. The stories in the brown notebook, which was almost full by now. The hours with Ludwig at the kitchen table, in which he had learned more about Berlin than in two years at university. None of it fitted into a table. And yet, he thought, as he shaped the dough, that was exactly the reason why he wanted the job.

The cover letter was harder. Andrei wrote seven versions. The first was too long, two pages full of enthusiasm about trams, which Lena called “moving, but unprofessional”. The second was too short and sounded, as Mara put it, “like a robot applying for asylum”. The third contained three grammar mistakes, which Ludwig marked with a red pen, with the same strictness with which Ingrid had corrected dictations for forty years. The fourth, fifth and sixth went into the bin without anyone being allowed to read them.

Mara gave him a piece of advice that she had been given herself five years earlier, when she applied to the hospital. “Don't write what you think they want to hear,” she said, when she came down for coffee with Jakob on Sunday. “Write what you can give them. Every day HR managers read a hundred cover letters that say: I am able to work in a team. Nobody believes that. But if you write that you get up at four every morning and have never been late, then they believe you.” Jakob nodded. “It's the same at our school,” he said. “The best applications are the ones where you can see the person.”

On the evening before the deadline, at eleven at night, Andrei was still sitting at the kitchen table in the first-floor flat, in front of his laptop, staring at the empty screen. Lena was already asleep; she had to be at the café at five. Through the open window came the warm June air and the scent of the lime trees in the courtyard. And then he heard a soft knocking from below, through the floor. Three times. It was the signal he and Ludwig had agreed on when he moved in: if Ludwig needed something, he would knock on the ceiling with his stick.

Andrei ran down the stairs, his heart in his mouth. But Ludwig wasn't ill. He was sitting in Ingrid's armchair, in his pyjamas, with a cup of tea and an old folder on his knees. “I heard you walking up and down upstairs,” he said. “For two hours. Nobody can stand that. Sit down. I want to show you something.”

Andrei sat down on the stool next to the tiled stove, which in June was of course cold, but still seemed to be the warmest place in the flat. Fritz lay in his basket, snoring. On the table was a plate with two slices of apple cake that Lena had brought down in the afternoon, and Ludwig pushed it towards Andrei without a word. “Eat,” he said. “You can't write good letters on an empty stomach. Ingrid used to say that too. Before every petition to the authorities she ate a slice of cake. She said sugar makes you brave.”

In the folder was Ludwig's own application to the Berlin transport company, from 1968. A single sheet, typed on an old typewriter, with two typing errors and a grease stain in the corner. Underneath, a handwritten CV, eight lines long. Born in 1948 in Berlin-Pankow. Primary school. Apprenticeship as a locksmith. Military service. And then, right at the bottom, a sentence that Ludwig, at nineteen, apparently hadn't been able to leave out: “I want to become a tram driver because as a child I rode the number 46 with my mother every day, and once the driver let me press the bell.”

The HR manager back then was called Mr Pohl. He read this sentence out loud at the interview, and I wanted the ground to swallow me up. And then he said: my boy, that's the only honest sentence I've read this week. You start on Monday.

Ludwig laughed at the memory. “I worked there for forty-one years after that. First at the East Berlin transport company, after the fall of the Wall at the BVG. I lived through three systems, four types of tram and eleven HR managers. But I still think of Mr Pohl today. He taught me that people aren't hired for their certificates, but for what they really want. Anyone can fake certificates. Not the wanting.” He tapped the old sheet gently with his finger. “You have the wanting, Andrei. You just have to write it down.”

Andrei read the sentence once more. Then he looked at Ludwig, who was smiling, and he understood. He had written six versions in which he had tried to sound like the perfect candidate: able to work in a team, able to work under pressure, reliable, with solid knowledge of everything. But he hadn't written a single honest sentence. Not one sentence that could only be his.

He went back upstairs and wrote the seventh version in an hour. It was one page long, with all the phrases Lena had shown him, with a subject line and reference number and “I would be very pleased to be invited”. He wrote about his studies, about the app he had developed for his master's, an app that showed blind people in Sibiu the way to the nearest bus stop. And then, in the second-to-last paragraph, he wrote a sentence he couldn't leave out.

Since February I have lived above a man who drove trams at the BVG for forty years. Today he no longer takes the tram, because the stops are too high for his knee, and the app doesn't tell him which stops are step-free. I want to improve the app so that he can ride the tram again. And together with him, everyone else who can't any more either.

He read the paragraph three times. Then he deleted it, because he thought it was too personal. Then he wrote it in again, word for word, because he realised that without this paragraph the letter sounded like the other six again. He thought of his mother in Sibiu, who had once told him: whoever hides is not found. And of Ludwig, who at nineteen had written that he had been allowed to press the bell. He left the paragraph as it was.

At half past twelve he clicked “Send”. Then he went to bed, lay down next to Lena and fell asleep at once, for the first time in a week without worries. Downstairs, in the ground-floor flat, Ludwig put the old folder back in the cupboard, next to the photo album and Susanne's tin box. He didn't know whether Andrei would get the job. But he knew that Mr Pohl, if he had still been alive, would have read that sentence out loud.

Two weeks later, on a hot Tuesday in July, an email came. Andrei read it in the bakery, with flour on his hands, and had to sit down on a sack of sugar. “Dear Mr Ionescu, thank you for your application. We would be pleased to meet you in person and warmly invite you to an interview on 15 July at 10 o'clock.” Underneath, in a different font, as if someone had added it afterwards: “PS: Please give our regards to your neighbour.”

Andrei ran, still with flour on his hands and his apron on, all the way along Kastanienallee home and knocked three times on Ludwig's window, just as Ludwig knocked on his ceiling. Ludwig opened it, read the email on the phone and said only: “Fifteenth of July. That's a Thursday. Mr Pohl hired me on a Thursday too.”
